lesson.title: NAFTA and the Free Trade Bet
lesson.summary: The North American Free Trade Agreement, which took effect in January 1994, eliminated most trade barriers between the United States, Canada, and Mexico and became a lasting symbol of the promises and costs of globalization.
lesson.body:
The idea of a North American free trade zone began under President Ronald Reagan and was negotiated in earnest under George H.W. Bush, but it fell to Bill Clinton to push the agreement through a skeptical Congress after taking office in 1993. The North American Free Trade Agreement, known as NAFTA, was signed by the leaders of the United States, Canada, and Mexico in December 1992, ratified by Congress in 1993, and took effect on January 1, 1994. It phased out tariffs and many other barriers to trade and investment among the three countries, creating one of the largest free trade zones in the world.

The debate over NAFTA cut across normal party lines. Independent presidential candidate Ross Perot warned during the 1992 campaign that the agreement would produce what he called a giant sucking sound as American manufacturing jobs moved south to lower wage Mexico. Labor unions and many Democrats in Congress opposed the deal for similar reasons, while most Republicans and the business community supported it. Clinton ultimately won approval by adding side agreements on labor standards and environmental protection meant to address some of these concerns, and by building a coalition that crossed party lines.

NAFTA fit naturally into the broader story of Clinton era globalization: a bet that removing barriers to trade would grow the overall economy, lower consumer prices, and strengthen ties among North American economies, even if the gains and losses fell unevenly. In the years that followed, trade among the three countries expanded enormously, and industries such as auto manufacturing became deeply integrated across the U.S. Mexico border through supply chains and assembly plants known as maquiladoras. At the same time, many American manufacturing communities, especially in the Midwest, did lose factory jobs to Mexico and to global competition more broadly, and economists still debate how much of that decline NAFTA caused compared with other forces like automation and competition from China. The controversy over NAFTA became a template for later fights over trade policy, and its legacy continued to shape debate for decades, including its eventual replacement by a new agreement between the three countries.
